items.content:
@zacharylipton @demishassabis When you work on research (particularly on long-term research), you have to accept the fact that corporate management, who is often interested in short-term impact, may think you are wasting your time and company resources. 
But it very much depends what you objectives and your horizon is.

- If your goal is keeping up with the current AI product race, then you might think that long-term bets are a waste.
- If your goal is "AGI" (whatever you mean by that) then your horizon is likely longer and your modus operandi is very different.
- However, If you think "AGI is just around the corner through LLM scaling", then you might think working on world models and other new AI concepts is a waste.
- But if you know that AGI requires a few more conceptual advances (as Demis and I do), you pick a role that maximizes progress towards that goal. That role is necessarily less connected with products, less connected with management, and more connected with research.
- I can't speak for Demis, but in my case, I've always been supportive of high-quality work on LLMs and impressed by the results. My personal interest was to advance towards human-level AI, and I never thought LLMs were the ticket. But I always thought LLMs were incredibly useful as a technology, and eventually as the centerpieces of a family of products.

As a high-level IC (not a manager), I would not have had the influence or power to stifle work on LLM even if I had wanted to (which I had not).

Yesterday me and my friends talked about the Dead Internet Theory

If nobody asks questions anymore on Stack Overflow, and sites like Reddit are now taken over by AI reply bots to promote brands, as well as AI reply bots on here, there is no real content anymore on the internet

And then there is no fresh training data anymore

I thought about something like, how would you find out the best outdoor action camera? Before I would search :

site:https://t.co/hzXOs1G2mg best outdoor action camera

But now I just ask my AI which is the best

The problem is if nobody creates new content anymore and just asks their AI every question, the AI has nothing to train on anymore

And then I thought so what will happen? Will you get companies with giant warehouses that just buy stuff and review it with manually or with humanoid robots? Will you get humanoid robots backpacking in South East Asia to get life experience as training data? Or will we all train it by giving it access to our AI chats and user data?

I don't know but I think it's likely the web will dead in the future and AI companies will have to find training data elsewhere

items.content:
Modern language models often improve through additional training after pretraining, but many current methods still depend on correct solutions, environmental feedback, or guidance from a stronger model, which makes self-improvement difficult when such supervision is expensive or unavailable.

The authors from @BytedanceTalk, @GeorgiaTech, @UCSanDiego, and @UofMaryland test whether a model can instead learn entirely from its own attempts.

Their method, U-OPSD, generates several solutions to each problem, uses the majority answer as a temporary target, and treats an agreeing solution as extra context for a “teacher” version of the same model; it then corrects the model along solutions that disagreed with that majority. This uses distillation—training one set of predictions to match another—but without labels, external feedback, or a separate teacher model. 

On five competition-math benchmarks, the method improves several Qwen3 models and, when the models are not already producing long reasoning traces, performs better on average than comparable methods trained with correct answers.

Ten talks on what breaks after the model gets good:

- Give people an AI that is confidently lying and they follow it nearly 80% of the time, against 92.7% when it is right. Human review is not the backstop you think it is
- GPT 5.5 declared a full repo refactor finished in 10 minutes 22 seconds. It had written 2,000 lines of scaffolding and no actual models
- Prompting an agent to behave is not a guardrail, because whoever prompt injects it can undo the instruction. Declare permissions instead, and let the automation do nothing
- A compromised litellm sat live for three hours harvesting API keys and SSH keys. It was caught because the malware crashed Cursor
- Everyone is shipping more and reaching fewer people. It is the newsletter author writing a book a week that nobody reads

https://t.co/VkGFDkkTRP

items.content:
I'm officially done reading AI-generated code.

It's been two weeks since I looked at any of it.

I think the IDE is officially on its way to the graveyard. The job is no longer about "writing code," so we need new tools that better reflect this new reality.

While reviewing the code, I realized my only complaints were stylistic, and I wasn't finding any obvious bugs anymore.

The more code I generated, the harder it became to keep track of every line. I found that my time is better spent designing ways to verify that the overall system works than looking at the code.

State-of-the-art coding agents are better at writing code than I'd ever be, and I'm going to stop pretending otherwise.

I still think these coding agents can't go too far without an experienced human guiding them, but we're past the point where we need to check every line of code.

items.content_html:
I'm officially done reading AI-generated code.

It's been two weeks since I looked at any of it.

I think the IDE is officially on its way to the graveyard. The job is no longer about "writing code," so we need new tools that better reflect this new reality.

While reviewing the code, I realized my only complaints were stylistic, and I wasn't finding any obvious bugs anymore.

The more code I generated, the harder it became to keep track of every line. I found that my time is better spent designing ways to verify that the overall system works than looking at the code.

State-of-the-art coding agents are better at writing code than I'd ever be, and I'm going to stop pretending otherwise.

I still think these coding agents can't go too far without an experienced human guiding them, but we're past the point where we need to check every line of code.

@wholemars I once was giving a speech to a bunch of Irish entrepreneurs who were in Silicon Valley to study why Google or Facebook starts in Silicon Valley and not in Ireland. The same is true of a bunch of different people: they didn't understand why Instagram was worth a billion dollars, much less worth $100 billion.

The day that I gave the speech to these people was the very day that Mark Zuckerberg bought Instagram for a billion dollars. Keep in mind, they didn't have a dollar in sales, they didn't have very many employees (I think they had 14 employees), they had no assets, and no profits. They just couldn't get it, and that explains the whole difference.

Europe is all about taxing Silicon Valley and not starting its own Silicon Valley. If they started their own Silicon Valley, they wouldn't do stupid shit like what they've been doing to us. They're all about extraction and taxing, rather than taking risks and changing their systems so that entrepreneurs can take risks. I hope it changes.

@simhskal Looking north, going across the Golden Gate Bridge, Sausalito really rocks. A little bit north of that, you could go to Muir Woods, but you need a ticket to get into the redwood trees. 

The coast anywhere, either north or south of San Francisco, is stunningly beautiful in both directions. 

If you're into wine, going to Napa is always a treat. Carmel, about two hours south, is a stunning little beach town that is worth spending a day in. To the east, Lake Tahoe and Yosemite National Park are stunning. There is so much to do.

And of course, there is all the stuff right in San Francisco: riding a cable car, going to Alcatraz, and doing all the touristy stuff.
